Moreover, we find that higher-order effects considerably increase the breakup cross section at low energies. Consequently, extracting radiative capture cross sections from the breakup reaction data in this case is extremely challenging. We suggest that the forward Coulomb breakup suppression is a general feature of collision processes involving $N=Z$ clustered nuclei. Our findings underscore the importance of advancing alternative indirect methods for nuclear reactions in astrophysics such as electron-induced dissociation.

papers.title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
papers.summary: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

papers.title: Supporting or Replacing Students' Reasoning? Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted Proof Learning
papers.summary: We studied 153 students in an undergraduate proof-based mathematics course with staggered-access to an AI support system. Students were randomly assigned to receive an AI chatbot and a homework-feedback interface earlier or later in the course. During the period when only the early-access group had access, their homework scores were 2.56 points higher, but exam performance did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that improved AI-supported homework performance did not translate into detectable gains on a subsequent exam. After all students received access, every additional 100 messages sent to the AI chatbot was associated with a 3.02-point lower score on the subsequent exam. A mediation analysis showed a significant indirect association linking lower baseline self-efficacy to greater chatbot use and, in turn, lower exam scores: a one-point decrease in self-efficacy corresponded to 0.62 fewer exam points through chatbot use. These findings raise concerns that students may use the chatbot to offload their cognitive reasoning. Use of the homework-feedback interface, which required students to submit their proof attempts before receiving feedback, was not negatively associated with exam performance. We recommend against using a chatbot for AI tutoring and suggest exploring a tutor embedded in the course activities.
papers.comment: 14 pages. This manuscript presents a substantially revised and extended analysis of the classroom study reported in arXiv:2602.18807 and the earlier preprint arXiv:2509.16778

papers.title: Chaotic dynamics and resonances in Einstein-Rosen standing wave spacetimes
papers.summary: Recent work has revealed chaotic geodesic behavior in Einstein-Rosen standing gravitational wave spacetimes. The dynamics of massive test particles are dominated by chaotic heteroclinic networks. This study demonstrates that the dynamical structure of the system is far richer than previously thought. Applying the subharmonic Melnikov function method to Poincaré maps reveals the admissible types of heteroclinic networks. I trace the evolution of these structures under the continuous change of the solution's parameters. In this way, I identify bifurcation phenomena, including a period-doubling bifurcation.

papers.title: How Different, or Different How? Stance Granularity in Viewpoint Selection for Dialog Systems that Engage Users with Alternative Views
papers.summary: Systems that aim to help a user engage with viewpoints other than their own have to decide how different those viewpoints should be. Viewpoints are mainly represented on a scalar scale, too coarse to distinguish viewpoints that disagree with the user about different things. We introduce a selection policy in which a bandit sets how far viewpoints may sit from the user, and the policy selects the most novel viewpoint within that bound. We vary only its stance encoder, comparing a scalar score with Perspectivized Stance Vectors, which break a position into separate stances on concepts. We integrate it inside a dialog system and run a between-subjects study (N=63). Concept-level stance produces more varied exposure sequences and broader coverage of the topic's positions, but does not change how deeply users justify viewpoints or how accurately they reconstruct them. Finally, we analyze user--viewpoint relations at the concept level, showing that users reconstruct a viewpoint least accurately on concepts that one side took no position on, rather than on concepts where the two disagreed. Our findings open up opportunities for dialog systems that support engagement with alternative viewpoints by acting on which concepts a user and a viewpoint disagree on, rather than on distance alone.

papers.title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
papers.summary: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.
papers.comment: 6 pages, presented at CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge

papers.title: Newtonian I-Love-Q relations: An enthalpy-based approach
papers.summary: We present a pedagogical introduction to the I-Love-Q relations within Newtonian gravity using an enthalpy-based formulation of stellar structure. Introducing the specific enthalpy converts Euler's equation into a first integral of hydrostatic equilibrium and recasts the equation of state as a relation between the mass density and the enthalpy. Together with Poisson's equation, these relations provide a unified description of spherical equilibrium and deformations induced by rotation and tides. We illustrate the formalism with polytropic equations of state and a relativistic free Fermi gas. In Newtonian gravity, slow uniform rotation and a weak tidal field excite the same linear quadrupolar response, yielding the exact identity $\bar I^{\,2}\bar Q/\barλ\equiv1$ for the dimensionless (``bar'') observables---independently of the equation of state. This exact identity is distinguished from the approximate universality of the pairwise I-Love-Q relations, whose residual dependence on stellar structure is illustrated by the models considered in this work.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures Submitted to European Journal of Physics

papers.title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
papers.summary: We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.

papers.title: Anisotropic spin hydrodynamics in a magnetized medium: entropy-current formulation and minimal linear modes
papers.summary: We formulate anisotropic relativistic spin hydrodynamics in a parity-even magnetized medium using an Israel--Stewart entropy-current construction. Treating the magnetic field at leading order in the gradient expansion reduces the rotational symmetry to $SO(2)$ and separates spin susceptibilities and dissipative transport into longitudinal, transverse, and mixed channels. A restricted quadratic entropy current yields transient equations for the retained dissipative stresses and spin fluxes. We analyze a minimal linear closure around an unpolarized homogeneous equilibrium, retaining dynamical magnetic-flux perturbations but no explicit spin-magnetization coupling; spin and magnetic fluctuations mix through the fluid variables. Infrared coefficient equations and ultraviolet characteristic expansions organize the magnetosonic and Alfvén-like spectra together with spectator spin-flux poles. The first-order truncation exhibits unstable boost-sector poles and superlinear large-wave-number branches, interpreted as diagnostics of the truncated equations rather than microscopic dispersion predictions. For the baseline parameters, finite relaxation times yield asymptotically linear propagation branches and finite relaxation poles, with no growing modes found on the sampled grid. The characteristic speeds depend nonmonotonically on spin transport and provide necessary light-cone diagnostics, without establishing general stability or strong hyperbolicity.

papers.title: $N \to Δ$ Transition Form Factors in the Thermal AdS/QCD Soft-Wall Model with Modified Propagators
papers.summary: We investigate electromagnetic (EM) and axial vector (AV) form factors of the nucleon-Delta baryon transition within the thermal AdS/QCD soft-wall model. While the vector bulk-to-boundary propagator admits a well-behaved analytical solution, the transverse axial vector equation of motion involves the vacuum expectation value of the bifundamental scalar (generating chiral symmetry breaking). Due to this, the axial propagator diverges asymptotically, rendering it unsuitable for computing observables in the soft-wall model. To address this problem, we implement a regularization for the axial propagator in the form of a momentum-dependent cut-off, that identifies its correct physical regime. This is achieved via an interior constraint approach to the boundary-value problem, that determines the cut-off point. The consistency of this procedure is verified near the UV limit. As a proof of concept, we test this modified propagator (and also a parametrically deformed version of it) to estimate axial vector form factors of the $N \to Δ$ transition, and find results moderately comparable with form factor profiles from experimental observations, lattice QCD, and other theoretical models. Equipped with this regularization, the thermal soft-wall model becomes a useful tool to probe thermal characteristics of QCD form factors. We demonstrate this for both, the EM and AV sectors of the $N \to Δ$ transition.

papers.title: In-Browser Human-AI Co-Writing for Counterspeech: An Exploratory User Study of Agency, Perceived Response Quality, and Time
papers.summary: Writing counterspeech that challenges online hate speech can be cognitively and emotionally demanding, whereas fully automated generation may weaken users' sense of voice and responsibility. We present an in-browser AI-assisted co-writing tool that enables users to contribute their own ideas and offers three editable suggestions generated by a large language model using dynamically retrieved hate speech-counterspeech examples from the Multitarget CONAN dataset. We evaluated the tool in an exploratory within-subject study with ten participants, complemented by think-aloud observations and semi-structured interviews with half of the participants. Participants wrote responses to three self-selected hate speech instances without assistance and then repeated the task with the tool. Final responses were subsequently peer-rated for empathy, non-toxicity, relevance, specificity, and persuasiveness. Participants evaluated the interface positively, and qualitative accounts linked user input, selection among alternatives, and small edits to perceived agency and responsibility. Assisted responses received higher descriptive mean ratings across all five proxies, with the largest difference for empathy. Mean composition time increased from 2.52 to 3.88 minutes. Qualitative findings further revealed a tension between empathy-oriented outputs and users' desire to express legitimate anger or direct disagreement. We contribute exploratory design guidance for treating AI-assisted counterspeech as deliberative co-writing rather than automated text production.
papers.comment: Pre-Publishing for the 10th Workshop on Online Abuse and Harm 2026

papers.title: Making Generative AI Workable at Work: Accountability, Localization, and Representation in Kenyan and Nigerian Small Businesses
papers.summary: Generative AI is widely framed as democratizing skilled work by lowering the barrier to producing professional output. Drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with 27 workers across 21 small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in Kenya and Nigeria (July to October 2023), we find that availability alone did not make participation workable. In participants' accounts, drafting was rarely the hard part. The consequential work was making AI-assisted drafts defensible enough to circulate to clients. We identify five intertwined practices through which participants made generative AI workable: using it as draft labour, steering outputs through iterative interaction, switching and comparing across tools, performing release work to make outputs accountable before circulation, and repairing context misfit when outputs failed local requirements. We make two central contributions. First, we specify release work as a distinct, boundary-facing form of accountability labour, evidenced through verification gates, traceability reconstruction when sources fail, and non-delegation boundaries that decide what can ship. Second, we show how localization and representational failures, which we call context misfit, operate in everyday work as a recurring breakdown-and-repair class, including failures of local language, institutional knowledge, and the credible representation of African people and places, and we document the repair repertoire they demanded. Reframing democratization as workable participation, we argue that reported gains were conditional on this accountability and repair labour, and we translate the findings into four design directions for workplace generative AI. We treat Kenya and Nigeria as two situated cases, not as a representative sample of SMBs or the Global South.

papers.title: Cognitively Constrained Partners for Zero-Shot Coordination in Real-Time Partitioned Control
papers.summary: Effective human-machine teaming requires agents that coordinate with unpredictable human partners. Reinforcement learning from live human feedback or large behavioural datasets is expensive, while purely simulated training overfits to artificial conventions and fails at Zero-Shot Coordination with real people. We propose a framework for training teaming agents against Cognitively Constrained Partners: simulated partners whose diversity emerges from procedural constraints grounded in human physiological literature, specifically reaction delays and perceptual limitations, rather than from reward shaping or historical training checkpoints. In a modified Lunar Lander environment, we report preliminary evidence that these partners play more like real people than unconstrained agents do, and that agents trained against them match the strongest cross-play baselines while being the only ones whose performance does not depend on how their training partners were generated. We also describe a human-participant study designed so that its rankings can be compared directly against cross-play, testing how well that standard evaluation predicts real human-agent teaming.
papers.comment: 30 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Human-AI Coevolution: Measuring Human-Agent Teams in the Agentic Era

papers.title: CoWriter: Guiding Methodological and Synergetic Human-LLM Co-Authoring
papers.summary: While LLMs have transformed text generation, standard chat-and-canvas interfaces often reduce human authoring to quite passive supervision, causing review fatigue, over-reliance on AI, and the sidelining of the human role in long-form, source-grounded writing. Prior systems typically address isolated writing phases, leaving comprehensive end-to-end human-LLM collaboration largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce CoWriter, a proactive agentic scheme that adapts expert human (co-)authoring methodologies from cognitive science to flexibly steer the entire writing workflow while actively encouraging the user to engage. In an exploratory user study, compared to a standard LLM baseline, authors using CoWriter better expressed their perspectives and maintained a higher sense of document ownership, supported quantitatively by $2.2\times$ more successful agent engagements. Furthermore, external reader judges rated the resulting texts higher in "human touch" qualities like storytelling and integrating unique personal experiences. Overall, our results demonstrate that proactively engaging users through established human practices is beneficial for effective LLM-supported co-authoring, providing useful methodologies, techniques and insights for future research on collaborative agents.

papers.title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding
papers.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.
papers.comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET), NeurIPS 2026

papers.title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
papers.summary: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.

papers.title: Beyond city pairs: Higher-order information in urban growth across borders
papers.summary: We apply higher-order information measures to urban growth across borders and spatial units. We analyse 8,808 functional urban areas using gridded GDP estimates allocated from national accounts. Negative estimated O-information occurs in 29.93% of cross-border triplets and 2.00% of domestic triplets. This fifteen-fold contrast falls to fourfold at comparable dependence strength and persists under data-quality restrictions. Target-specific decompositions show how information overlaps or combines across cities. Administrative subdivisions have mean O-information within matched random-map ranges inside countries. These findings show why interpreting geographic dependence requires specifying comparison cities and spatial units, while economic connections remain to be established independently.

papers.title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities
papers.summary: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and able to resist perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Theoretical approaches to this problem typically require making strict assumptions about the structure, parameters and functional forms used in models, hindering general insight. Here, we address this problem by developing and analyzing a generalized model of microbial community dynamics, capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach allows us to assess the stability of microbial systems across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure and non-linear dynamics. Our analysis shows how community stability is constrained by system size and identifies its key metabolic and dynamical drivers, highlighting the central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity. Furthermore, we show how the structure of communities mediates their stability, allowing communities to counteract the destabilizing cross-feeding loops through organization into hierarchical trophic structures. Together, these results provide new insight into the stability of microbial communities and offer a flexible analytical framework for future work to explore the responses of communities to perturbation.

papers.title: Intraday Forecasting Ability and Liquidity Provision of Institutional Traders
papers.summary: This study uses a high-frequency dataset from a stock exchange to examine how forecasting ability and liquidity provision relate to institutional traders' proprietary intraday profitability. We discover persistent forecasting abilities among traders. Specifically, we demonstrate that hypothetical flow-following strategies based on the execution flows of these skillful traders yield annualized Sharpe ratios ranging from 16 to 63 across various trading frequencies. We match buy and sell executions into positions, linking realized profit and loss (P&L) to horizon-matched forecasting proxies and the liquidity roles of both executions. Our findings indicate a direct correlation between improved forecasting ability and profitability, where a one-standard-deviation increase in the forecasting ability proxy is associated with 1.02 -- 1.19 currency units higher P&L per matched position. Additionally, we measure liquidity-provision intensity within a matched position by its number of passive executions: zero, one, or two. In these regressions, P&L is 1.28 -- 1.31 currency units higher for one passive execution than for none, and a further 3.79 -- 3.82 higher for two than for one, underscoring the significant financial benefits of liquidity provision.

papers.title: Music Between Two Minds: Individual Signatures, Shared States, and the Emergence of Creative Interaction
papers.summary: Some of the most valued forms of human creativity arise between people-in conversation, collaboration, and improvised music-yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time remains unknown. Here we examined the information dynamics of interpersonal improvisation using 986 professional jazz improvisations. Pitch-based fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise behaved as signatures of individual identity: the two partners differed within 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos and the separation between partners persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm-based fluctuations showed the reverse organization: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take yet shifted together from take to take, and this shared state drifted gradually as each performance progressed, with each performer moving away from their own past at the same rate as from their partner's. Beyond joint drift, solo hand-offs revealed turn-by-turn complementarity: when one performer exceeded their own average surprise in the predictive dynamics of improvisation, the partner's next solo fell below their own, in both pitch and rhythm and in all duos. Improvising pairs thus neither fuse into one system nor remain two independent ones: they preserve individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull continually rebalances their interaction. Individuality and togetherness thus coexist, carried by different musical dimensions, a measurable organization of creativity that emerges between minds.

papers.title: Parton distribution functions of the proton in a hot isospin-asymmetric nuclear medium and finite nuclei
papers.summary: When a nucleon is bound in a nucleus, its quark distributions are modified, and the change in the spin-dependent distributions can differ in size from that in the spin-independent ones. We compute the unpolarized $f_1(x)$, helicity $g_1(x)$, and transversity $h_1(x)$ distributions of the $u$ and $d$ quarks in a proton immersed in hot and isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter. The proton is described in the diquark spectator model, with the medium effects entering through the effective quark, diquark, and proton masses computed using the chiral SU(3) quark mean field (CQMF) model. The axial and tensor charges are obtained for baryon densities up to saturation density and temperatures $T = 0$ and $0.1$ GeV, in both symmetric nuclear matter and pure neutron matter. The distributions are then carried to $^{40}$Ca, $^{56}$Fe, $^{197}$Au, and $^{208}$Pb at zero temperature through the local density approximation. In symmetric matter at saturation density and zero temperature, the peaks of the three $u$ quark distributions move toward larger $x$ and fall least for the unpolarized distribution and most for the transversity distribution, so the spin-dependent $u$ quark distributions are modified more strongly. Between vacuum and saturation density, the axial charge of the proton drops from $1.28$ to $0.844$, and the tensor charge of the $u$ quark decreases while that of the $d$ quark grows in magnitude. At the center of each nucleus, the axial charge of the proton rises from $0.699$ in $^{40}$Ca to $0.817$ in $^{208}$Pb as the central baryon density decreases, which suggests that the modification at the center follows the central density rather than the mass number.

papers.title: Testing for peer effects in short panels without identifying the network structure
papers.summary: We propose an instrument-based test for peer effects in short-T panels when the underlying network is unknown. The test avoids estimating the network by aggregating pairwise comparisons between covariate-projected outcomes of potential peers and residualized own outcomes. The statistic is designed for fixed-T, large-N settings with individual fixed effects, heterogeneous slopes, heteroskedasticity, and serial dependence within units. We also develop a weighted extension that accounts for additive common time effects. The limiting distribution is standard Gaussian when the norm of the projected component of the outcomes is bounded away from zero, but can be nonstandard when it is local to zero. We derive a conditional Gaussian limit experiment and a feasible conditional Monte Carlo procedure to obtain uniformly valid critical values. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the conditional procedure leads to accurate size control while retaining power against latent peer-effect alternatives.

papers.title: Directionally Correct Views in Portfolio Optimization
papers.summary: Portfolio optimization techniques often use historical data to estimate parameters for Markowitz-type or ML models. Effective allocation requires a way to align the available data with conditions expected over the investment horizon. Inspired by the Black-Litterman framework, we ask whether incorporating expert views leads to better portfolio allocations. In a simple Markowitz setting, we show that even a small amount of directionally correct information can materially improve investment decisions. We also discuss how expert views can be incorporated in end-to-end portfolio models using entropy-based ideas. Somewhat surprisingly, our empirical results indicate that simpler Markowitz-type model perform as well as an end-to-end model, once directionally correct experts are incorporated.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, accepted at NeuRIPS MLxOR workshop 2026

papers.title: Multichoice Modeling: Exploring Decision Configuration Space under Uncertainty
papers.summary: Decision support has become sophisticated at exploring uncertainty, but much less so at representing the architecture of the decision itself. As a result, the decision space is often narrowed before uncertainty is analyzed, leaving interactions among choices and the effects of alternatives they imply largely invisible. This paper introduces multichoice modeling, a framework for making large decision configuration spaces explicit and computationally explorable under uncertainty. Drawing on the logic of rugged landscapes, we conceptualize such problems as contingent performance landscapes, where interdependent choices generate configuration-specific outcomes whose value changes across uncertain futures. The computational framework combines multidimensional decision and uncertainty spaces in a single simulation. Further, variance-based sensitivity analysis is used for identifying influential choices, and conditional distribution analysis for comparing configuration-specific performance profiles. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies: a manufacturing process upgrade, M&A strategy, and mortgage design. By contrasting conventional uncertainty-only analysis with multichoice modeling, the cases show how opening the decision configuration space can reveal unexpected complementarities, near-best configurations with different risk profiles, and strategies that were not apparent as alternatives at the outset.

papers.title: Lifetime of the singly charged $^{229}$Th nuclear isomer
papers.summary: The nucleus of thorium-229 ($^{229}$Th) has an exceptionally low-energy isomeric state ($^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th). Because its excitation energy is close to the energy levels of valence electrons, the lifetime of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th varies substantially depending on its electronic state. Although internal conversion and radiative decay were recently observed, the electronic bridge decay of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th, a higher-order decay process through an electronic transition, has not yet been confirmed. A promising candidate to search for this decay channel is singly charged $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ in the electronic ground state. Here we produce $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ by a charge exchange reaction in an ion trap and detect the isomers through measuring the electrons emitted from internal conversion processes. We determined the half-life of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ to be 0.46(8) s. Our result differs by several orders of magnitude from the half-lives of internal conversion and radiative decay, indirectly suggesting the existence of the electronic bridge decay of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th. This will enable the direct observation and further investigation of the electronic bridge process, which will contribute to understanding nuclear-electron interactions and accelerating nuclear deexcitation in the operation of a thorium-based nuclear clock.

papers.title: Risk Sensitivity and Stationary Equilibrium in Incomplete Markets
papers.summary: We study stationary equilibrium and comparative statics in an incomplete market economy with risk-sensitive preferences. We prove that a stationary equilibrium exists for every nonnegative degree of risk sensitivity. With independent income, greater risk sensitivity weakly raises aggregate saving at fixed prices and weakly lowers the smallest and the largest equilibrium interest rates. With stochastically monotone Markov income, these comparisons hold when the lower risk-sensitivity parameter is sufficiently small or the upper parameter sufficiently large. For pairs of intermediate values, however, greater risk sensitivity can lower saving, contrary to an existing result in the literature, and can raise the smallest and largest equilibrium rates. An exact decomposition identifies the forces driving these reversals.

papers.title: Equilibria and Learning in Competitive Market Making
papers.summary: We propose a market-making game played among $N \ge 2$ strategic market makers and a single non-strategic representative trader. In a continuous quote space, standard finite-game arguments do not apply, while non-convex and discontinuous payoffs rule out classical continuous existence results and complicate learning. Nonetheless, we characterize pure-strategy Nash equilibria (PSNEs) and show that at least one PSNE always exists under minimal assumptions on the underlying asset value distribution, and that the equilibrium bid-ask spread widens strictly with asset value volatility. To obtain a tractable learning framework, we discretize prices and, under an additional regularity condition, show that the time-averaged play of no-internal-regret learners approaches the continuous Nash price envelope as the tick size vanishes. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations.

papers.title: The Reaction of Financial Markets to the Releases of DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K3: A Critical Analysis
papers.summary: This paper compares financial-market reactions to the releases of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025 and Kimi K3 in July 2026. Both AI models were presented as credible Chinese competitors near the capability frontier, but their releases conveyed different economic information. DeepSeek R1 combined open weights with unusually low reported training and inference costs, prompting investors to reassess expected demand for computing infrastructure and producing large stock-price decreases among semiconductor and data-centre-related firms. Kimi K3 instead entered at broadly frontier prices and generated a market reaction concentrated more heavily among rival Chinese AI laboratories. Drawing on descriptive event-window evidence, model capability and cost comparisons, subsequent industry developments, and the historical diffusion of open-source software, the paper argues that open-weight models redistribute rents across the AI value chain rather than eliminating them. Incumbents remain protected by complementary assets including distribution, product bundling, switching costs, proprietary data, serving capacity, and contractual trust. The analysis suggests that investors and policy makers should assess risks looking not only at model capability, but also at the ownership and durability of complementary assets across the AI value chain.

papers.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
papers.summary: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.

papers.title: From Turing Patterns to Spike Self-Replication and Nucleation in a Growing-Domain Tulip Breaking Virus Model
papers.summary: A recently proposed reaction-diffusion model for the tulip breaking virus (TBV) has been shown to generate striped pigmentation patterns on growing tulip petals. In this paper, we investigate the formation of localized spike patterns in this model in the asymptotic limit of small viral diffusivity. It is known that two distinct bifurcation mechanisms can occur which generate new spikes as the domain half-length $L$ slowly increases: spike self-replication and spike nucleation. Self-replication occurs through a saddle-node bifurcation of the inner spike core problem, whereas nucleation is associated with a fold of the nonlinear outer problem. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive critical conditions for these mechanisms and construct phase diagrams that predict which mechanism occurs first as $L$ increases, or whether nucleation is absent. We further combine these results with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state to obtain a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms. An interesting finding is that, for the TBV model, the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible. These results provide further insight into the mechanisms underlying the formation and evolution of pigmentation patterns in virus-infected tulips.

papers.title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
papers.summary: We give a self-contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass-action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yields a finite-minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn-Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded-speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 1 figure. Lean 4 formalization: https://github.com/BitMiracle-AI/detailed-balance-gac (tag v1.0). Use of AI tools is described in the Acknowledgements

papers.title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
papers.summary: Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost. On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources. We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it. The direction is a theorem at every error tolerance and held without exception in 23,545 draws, so which references are missing matters more than how many. Two adversarially chosen references suffice, at the median, to destroy uniqueness of the minimum explanation, and that number does not grow with panel size (Spearman 0.203, p = 0.15, over 20 to 353 references) where random loss scales linearly. Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%. That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. Published distance estimates exceed it in 296 of 296 cases. The mixture inferred by the published heuristic reproduces real observations better than the configuration that generated them in 282 of 296. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. It is unobservable through a point estimate of the count. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary appendices (32 pages) are included as an ancillary file. Code, exact input fixtures and saved run records: https://github.com/Haotian-Tang/recomb2027-pdd

papers.title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
papers.summary: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

papers.title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
papers.summary: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

papers.title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
papers.summary: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

papers.title: Shorter but not more catalytic: an active-site-resolved model of how tau reshapes amyloid-$β$ secondary nucleation
papers.summary: Tau cross-seeding creates a mechanistic puzzle. Tau fibrils accelerate amyloid-$β$42 (A$β$42) nucleation and produce a larger population of shorter A$β$ fibrils, yet homotypic secondary nucleation occurs at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly over fibril mass. Does making more, shorter fibrils make the A$β$ population more catalytic? A coupled tau-A$β$ model is extended to track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites exposed after plaque consolidation. The model recovers the preceding plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites form in direct proportion to fibril mass. At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: the departure of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so the extra fibrils matter only if each birth event introduces about as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is controlled mainly by a Damkohler number comparing monomer consumption by elongation with monomer clearance. Tau coupling increases homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation becomes the dominant monomer sink. In a composite scenario, these regimes occur in sequence. Across all cases examined, including 800 Latin-hypercube samples and simulations with mean fibril lengths of 0.3-30 $μm$, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure. The model predicts that shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed; matched-mass site counting and secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternatives.

papers.title: CREMA: Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms
papers.summary: The Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms (CREMA) setup has been developed and commissioned at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Laboratory for Nuclear Science. The instrument combines the Doppler-suppressed resolution of the collinear fast-beam geometry with the selectivity of resonance ionization, for precision measurements of hyperfine structure and isotope shifts in atoms and molecules. We describe the setup, including the ion-optical simulations in which a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm provided the starting settings for the beam transport, and report commissioning measurements of the hyperfine structure of 133Cs. The extracted hyperfine constants agree with literature values within one standard deviation, demonstrating the operational readiness of the setup. CREMA mirrors the Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Experiment at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams and serves as its offline counterpart for the development of laser ionization schemes and techniques for future studies of exotic atoms and molecules.

papers.title: Modelling Toxin-Induced Intraspecific Personality Variation in Predator-Prey Dynamics
papers.summary: Personality traits, such as boldness and shyness, can affect interspecific interactions through differences in individual behaviour. Environmental toxins may also alter these traits. However, few predator-prey models have considered animal personality. In this study, we extend a toxin-dependent predator-prey model by incorporating personality variation in both prey and predators. Prey personality affects birth and growth, whereas predator personality affects the predator functional response. The model is parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey exposed to methylmercury. Numerical results show that prey and predator personality have different effects on population dynamics. Prey personality tends to reduce biomass fluctuations and promote stable coexistence. In contrast, predator personality can increase biomass fluctuations and lead to persistent population oscillations. These effects are mainly observed at low and intermediate toxin concentrations that are environmentally relevant to freshwater ecosystems. Using a quasi-steady-state approximation, we reduce the model to a two-dimensional system and study its positivity, boundedness, and the existence of equilibria. The equilibrium structure depends jointly on the toxin level and the prey and predator personality contrasts. Based on this existence classification, we numerically investigate the local stability of all feasible equilibria and identify parameter regions corresponding to locally stable extinction, prey-only persistence, coexistence, and bistability. Overall, toxin-induced personality variation can qualitatively change predator-prey dynamics.
papers.comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Journal of Theoretical Biology

papers.title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
papers.summary: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.

papers.title: Thermomagnetic enhancement of conserved-charge correlations in a lattice-constrained PNJL model
papers.summary: Conserved-charge correlations offer a promising probe of magnetic fields in strongly interacting matter. We investigate their magnetic response and the finite-density equation of state within a lattice-constrained three-flavor Polyakov--Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model. A thermomagnetic scalar coupling, inferred by Gaussian process regression from lattice QCD results for the average light-quark condensate, incorporates inverse magnetic catalysis into the effective interaction. Without fitting conserved-charge observables, the resulting framework substantially improves their magnetic-field dependence and crossover behavior compared with the fixed-coupling model. In particular, it captures the pronounced magnetic enhancement of the baryon--electric-charge correlation and related susceptibility ratios, supporting their use as QCD magnetometers. The comparison demonstrates that the medium dependence of the effective interaction is essential to describe this response within the model. We further calculate pressure Taylor coefficients through sixth order and reconstruct the pressure and baryon density at nonzero baryon chemical potential. Our results show that lattice information from a single chiral observable constrains a broad thermodynamic response, connecting inverse magnetic catalysis, conserved-charge correlations, and the equation of state in a common framework. This provides a lattice-constrained basis for investigating magnetic-field signatures and finite-density thermodynamics in QCD matter.

papers.title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
papers.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.
papers.comment: Accepted (non-archival) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops Sim2Science and Interp4Discovery. Code: https://github.com/Shrivatsa-Deshmukh/sbi-gate-vs-ablation

papers.title: Machine Learning Neutrino-Nucleus Cross Sections II: More Leptons
papers.summary: Neutrino-nucleus cross sections are essential inputs for long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, yet remain challenging to model with high precision. Recent work demonstrated that fully black-box data-driven cross-section models cannot accurately generalize between near- and far-detector fluxes, but imposing Standard-Model symmetries via structure-function parameterizations provides a well-posed learning problem in a simplified DUNE-inspired muon-neutrino disappearance analysis. Here, we extend this framework to multiple lepton flavors and both neutrino and antineutrino beam modes, incorporating the electron appearance channel and enabling a simultaneous determination of $\sin^2θ_{23}$, $Δm^2_{31}$, and the CP-violating phase $δ_{\rm CP}$. We find that the learned cross section model recovers the injected oscillation parameters without significant bias, with constraints comparable to those obtained using the exact underlying cross section. Flux uncertainties have more significant effects in the multi-channel case, and incorporating flux nuisance parameters into the learning problem is required for accurate results. Our results demonstrate that this data-driven approach can be extended to the multi-channel measurements needed for long-baseline neutrino oscillation analyses.

papers.title: Probing imperfect axions with nuclear clocks
papers.summary: We show that $^{229}$Th nuclear clocks can probe departures from the Peccei-Quinn (PQ) solution to the strong CP problem. Explicit PQ breaking or additional CP-violating interactions can shift the minimum of the axion potential and generate CP-violating couplings to matter, inducing a clock response linear in the axion field. We investigate explicit PQ breaking and quark chromo-electric dipole operators as representative realizations of these \textit{imperfect axion} scenarios, consistent with electric dipole moment constraints. For axion dark matter, the linear signal oscillates at the Compton frequency and can dominate the quadratic response. Even without axion dark matter, the Earth can source a static axion field, enabling fifth-force searches with nuclear clocks.

papers.title: General-purpose equations of state for hadron-quark matter: first application to accretion-induced phase transitions in neutron stars
papers.summary: Strong first-order phase transitions in the cores of neutron stars (NSs) can have profound implications for astrophysical observables, however, their existence remains an open question. Since most NSs form in binary systems, they are expected to experience prolonged episodes of mass accretion that gradually increase their central density and can potentially trigger such a transition. This might, in turn, generate observable multi-messenger signals, as suggested by previous studies. Motivated by this prospect, we generate a new set of equations of state for hadron--quark matter with first-order phase transitions of various strengths, including neutrino absorption opacities in the quark phase as well. We then perform general-relativistic radiation hydrodynamics simulations of NSs undergoing accretion-induced phase transitions. In contrast to previous findings, our results indicate that these systems do not produce unbound ejecta for the models considered, making accretion-induced phase transitions unlikely sources of observable electromagnetic transients. However, we find that transitions are accompanied by intense neutrino emission, with peak luminosities reaching $\sim10^{52}~\mathrm{erg/s}$ for the strongest transition considered. To facilitate future numerical studies, we make the family of equations of state and neutrino opacities used in this work publicly available, enabling the systematic exploration of the role of the phase transition strength.

papers.title: Heavy-Quark Dynamics from $D^{0}$-Meson Anisotropy-Response Scaling Violations
papers.summary: A species-resolved anisotropy-response scaling framework is used to investigate heavy-quark dynamics through the elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) azimuthal anisotropies of $D^0$ mesons. The independently constrained light-flavor response provides a direct null test: the transformed $D^0$ harmonics exhibit approximate inter-harmonic closure but remain systematically displaced from the kaon-anchored scaling function, revealing a charm scaling violation. The common response is recovered through a charm-specific attenuation rescaling, $k_c$, together with a small low-$p_T$ hadronic-rescattering correction, $ζ_{\rm hs}\simeq0.06$, while retaining the established light-flavor prescription. In Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$~TeV, $k_c$ decreases from approximately $2.0$ in central and mid-central collisions to $1.27$ in the 30--50\% interval. For $D^0$ $v_2$, ultra-central p+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=8.16$~TeV require $k_c\simeq1.5$, whereas Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$~GeV are consistent with $k_c\simeq1$. The transition momentum exhibits a distinct system dependence: $D^0$ and light mesons show comparable $p_{T,\rm tr}\simeq4.5$--$5.0$~GeV/$c$ in Pb+Pb, consistent with the common large-system prescription also used in Au+Au, whereas p+Pb $D^0$ measurements are consistent with the lower light-meson scale of approximately $1.6$~GeV/$c$. These complementary constraints on attenuation strength and transition momentum provide a differential benchmark for heavy-quark transport and medium evolution.

papers.title: Relative geometry of nuclear mean fields through differential forms
papers.summary: Proton and neutron densities can have similar multipole moments while differing locally. We use differential forms to measure and locate such differences between nuclear mean fields. A pair invariant measures the angle between two density gradients, weighted by their magnitudes, and the coarea formula resolves its contribution over level surfaces. A triple invariant factorizes exactly into a weighted pair term and a directional term that measures the variation of a third field along the level-surface intersections. We test these quantities in 98 magnetized Wigner-Seitz solutions, five static Hartree-Fock configurations, an illustrative $^{16}$O + $^{34}$Mg collision, and periodic nuclear pasta (a slab and a connected network). The pair invariant distinguishes cell solutions with comparable proton quadrupole moments and is 253 times larger in $^{34}$Mg than in $^{24}$Mg; refinement to 0.6 fm changes it by at most 1.3% in the four configurations recomputed. The directional factor separates the sampled triaxial configurations from the prolate ones. In the collision, it accounts for the 7.3-fold rise of the triple before the first recorded low-density connection, while the weighted pair term changes by at most 3%. In nuclear pasta, slab and network configurations have similar integrated proton-neutron misalignment but different distributions over density levels; their triple invariants differ by a factor of about 370 on the finer grid, mainly due to the variation of the Coulomb potential along joint density levels. These comparisons require no preferred origin or axis. A resolved nonzero triple excludes a common symmetry axis, but zero does not establish one. The pasta results require further convergence studies.

papers.title: NTL amplification in a SuperCDMS-style detector fabricated from a University of South Dakota-grown germanium crystal
papers.summary: Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) amplification enables eV-sub-keV detection thresholds for low-mass dark-matter and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering experiments. We evaluated two University of South Dakota (USD)-grown germanium crystals fabricated as SuperCDMS-style four-channel athermal-phonon detectors and operated near 10 mK. The crystals had electrically active impurity concentrations near $10^10~\mathrm^-3$ and etch-pit densities of $300$-$7000~\mathrm^-2$. Contact-free biasing produced no resolvable amplification. However, after depositing a 600 nm aluminum bias contact, Detector~2 exhibited clear voltage-dependent NTL gain. The reconstructed channel-B energy increased from approximately 3.9 keV at 0 V to 34.9 keV at 40 V, corresponding to an 8.9-fold enhancement. Statistical centroid uncertainties were below 0.3%, while low-bias fits yielded effective prompt- and NTL-phonon response coefficients of $(6.77\pm0.82)%$ and $(4.77\pm0.20)%$, respectively, excluding systematic uncertainties. These results demonstrate the feasibility of USD-grown germanium for SuperCDMS-style high-voltage phonon detectors and highlight the importance of both crystal quality and contact fabrication in achieving NTL amplification.

papers.title: B$_{4/2}$ anomaly related to the shape coexistence in $^{94}$Zr
papers.summary: Solutions of the Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian with a sixth-order anharmonic oscillator potential, for both axially-symmetric and $γ$-unstable deformations, are applied to investigate the lowest states of the $^{94}$Zr nucleus. The experimentally observed $B_{4/2}$ anomaly is explained, within the present approach, by the presence of a coexistence between an approximately spherical shape ($2_{1}^{+}$) and an axially-symmetric deformed one ($4_{1}^{+}$). On the other hand, the energies of the $0_{2}^{+}$ and $2_{2}^{+}$ states and their associated electromagnetic transitions fit better a dynamical triaxial deformation configuration ($γ$-unstable). This overall picture of the lowest states in $^{94}$Zr corresponds to a triple shape coexistence scenario.

papers.title: Nuclear Geometry-Driven Femtoscopic Correlations in Light-Ion Collisions
papers.summary: Recent anisotropic flow measurements in $^{16}\rm O{+}^{16}\rm O$ and $^{20}\rm Ne{+}^{20}\rm Ne$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.36~TeV provide evidence for nuclear geometry-driven collectivity. In this Letter, we investigate the femtoscopic signatures of nuclear geometry in these light-ion collision systems, using a hybrid simulation framework that couples \textit{ab initio} nuclear configurations to viscous hydrodynamics and hadronic transport. We show that the $\rm Ne{+}Ne/O{+}O$ ratio of the freeze-out eccentricity, extracted from azimuthally sensitive femtoscopy, reaches 1.5-1.8 in central collisions for deformed nuclear configurations, compared with about unity for a spherical baseline. This enhancement is significantly larger than that of elliptic flow in the same simulations, and remains stable when pre-equilibrium free streaming is omitted, even though the absolute source radii change considerably. Confronting these predictions with future data will provide new, complementary constraints on nuclear structure and initial-condition modeling.
